lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Owned the weekly carrier scorecards for the regional managers and the monthly review meeting that discussed them.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites by redesigning slotting rules with the floor supervisors and retraining 45 pickers on the new layout.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: Experience should appear above Education.
items.because: Five years of full-time work should carry the page rather than giving the MBA the first substantive position.

items.says: The Experience section is not in reverse chronological order.
items.because: Crestline appears above the more recent Harbor Payments internship, breaking a standard scanning pattern.

items.says: Coastal Marine Services should be shortened or its relevance explained because it reads as unrelated.
items.because: The diesel-mechanic detail can distract from the product, operations and consulting narrative.

items.says: The wording attributes the entire under-five-day dry-dock turnaround to rebuilding engines and gearboxes.
items.because: Other repairs, testing, parts availability and dock logistics also determine total dry-dock time.

items.says: “Owned” describes an assigned responsibility, while the meeting phrase awkwardly buries the actual action.
items.because: The wording does not show what was done in the review and makes the scope of ownership unclear.

items.says: The forecast-error result appears after the cadence, cross-functional scope and method.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the reduction from 18% to 11%, which is the strongest evidence.

items.says: “Quarterly” and “12 consecutive quarters” repeat the same cadence information.
items.because: One phrase adds little evidence and uses space that could support the result or scope.

items.says: The 1,800-driver-hour result appears after a long chain of implementation details.
items.because: The annual driver-hour saving is the clearest proof of value but is harder to find at the end.

items.says: “Cutting” attributes the reduction in time to first payment to the redesigned verification step without a control or comparison method.
items.because: The figures show an observed reduction but do not necessarily establish that the redesign caused it.

items.says: The line treats support-ticket volume as RICE Reach without defining it as a proxy or specifying a period and deduplication.
items.because: Standard RICE Reach estimates distinct users or customers, while raw ticket counts can include repeat contacts.

items.says: The line does not say what changed because of the RICE prioritization.
items.because: It shows the decision process but not the resulting decision, adoption or business effect.

items.says: “RICE” is unexplained jargon for readers outside product management.
items.because: The acronym slows interpretation of the prioritization decision.

items.says: The long method list before the roadmap decision makes the result easy to miss.
items.because: The work reads more like a task list than evidence of product judgment.

items.says: The line reports a session-randomized result as an effect on merchants’ customers.
items.because: Session randomization estimates session-level conversion, and the same customer may appear in multiple sessions or both variants.

items.says: The five-point conversion lift lacks a defined conversion measure and comparison.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether five points means percentage points, relative percent or another unit, or what event was measured.

items.says: The checkout A/B test and its five-point conversion lift are duplicated from another bullet.
items.because: Repeating the same experiment and result consumes space without adding evidence.

items.says: “To 3,100 students” does not identify what was measured.
items.because: It is unclear whether the students were reached, eligible, registered or active users.

items.says: The bullet gives no product-lead contribution beyond launching the app.
items.because: A specific product or execution detail would distinguish the contribution from a generic launch claim.

items.says: “That would have been thrown away” buries the concise food-rescue outcome.
items.because: The relative clause slows the scan and keeps the 9-tonne result from standing out sooner.

items.says: The claimed 150% increase from 400 to 1,150 weekly active users is arithmetically wrong.
items.because: The increase is 750 divided by 400, or 187.5%.

items.says: The change from 75% to 95% is 20 percentage points, not a 20% increase.
items.because: The relative increase is approximately 26.7%, so the current wording is technically inaccurate.

items.says: “$2.4M annual saving” presents a modeled estimate as an actual saving.
items.because: Funding a pilot from the model does not establish that the saving was realized.

items.says: “Sized a $2.4M annual saving” is awkward phrasing.
items.because: Savings are usually estimated or quantified rather than sized.

items.says: The adoption result appears after the process details.
items.because: The passive construction makes the candidate’s action and the outcome harder to distinguish.

items.says: The pilot-approval outcome appears after the presentation method.
items.because: The approved pilot is the clearest evidence of client influence and should be easier to scan.

items.says: “The final recommendation” does not identify the recommendation’s substantive content.
items.because: The reader cannot connect the presentation to the scheduling solution described elsewhere.

items.says: The hospital’s approval or funding of a scheduling pilot is duplicated in two bullets.
items.because: The repeated outcome uses space without showing an additional result.
